base_properties.human_readable: Magisterial Integralist Reading: AI Governance Bound by Catholic Anthropology and Church Authority

stakeholders.name: the_magisterium
stakeholders.situation: Issues encyclicals, dicastery documents, and pastoral guidance (e.g. Rome Call for AI Ethics) claiming interpretive authority over what counts as dignity-respecting AI. Convenes signatories, negotiates with governments and firms, and adjudicates doctrinal conformity of proposed technology governance frameworks. Its authority rests on claimed continuity with apostolic teaching, not on enforceable civil sanction.

stakeholders.name: vulnerable_populations
stakeholders.situation: Includes the elderly, disabled, and economically precarious who are disproportionately exposed to algorithmic sorting, automated denial of services, and surveillance. The reading's insistence on embodied, relational personhood is offered as a check against being reduced to a data profile or optimization target; they have no independent capacity to enforce this protection and depend on Church advocacy and allied civil-society pressure.

stakeholders.name: industrial_workers
stakeholders.situation: Workers facing automation-driven displacement are named beneficiaries of the doctrine's labor-dignity principles (drawing on Rerum Novarum and Laborem Exercens lineage), which argue AI deployment must be subordinated to the dignity of work and just wages rather than pure efficiency. Benefit is rhetorical and organizing leverage more than binding legal protection; exit from labor markets under automation pressure remains constrained regardless of doctrinal advocacy.

stakeholders.name: families_and_children
stakeholders.situation: Framed as needing protection from AI systems (companion bots, algorithmic curation, reproductive and genetic technologies) that the reading holds threaten formation of relational, embodied identity. They cannot select out of the technological environment; their benefit depends entirely on whether the Church's moral suasion actually changes what gets built and deployed.

stakeholders.name: technocratic_platform_elites
stakeholders.situation: Executives and engineering leadership at major AI firms are named as bearing reputational and, in aspirational cases, regulatory costs if the Magisterium's anthropological framework gains purchase in policy circles (EU AI Act consultations, UN discussions, state-level legislation informed by Catholic-aligned lobbying). They retain substantial exit — they can ignore, selectively co-opt (signing symbolic pledges), or route around doctrinal pressure via jurisdictions where it has no political traction — so the cost is reputational and selective rather than structural.

stakeholders.name: transhumanist_researchers
stakeholders.situation: Researchers and advocacy organizations pursuing cognitive enhancement, life-extension, and human-AI merger technologies are directly named as antagonists in Church teaching, which holds their project as a rejection of creaturely finitude. They bear stigma and exclusion from Catholic-aligned funding, academic, and policy venues, but retain full capacity to pursue their research programs in secular or techno-optimist-friendly jurisdictions and institutions.

stakeholders.name: secular_ai_ethicists
stakeholders.situation: Scholars working from rights-based, consequentialist, or procedural frameworks find their approaches treated by this reading as metaphysically thin or parasitic on a Christian anthropology they decline to acknowledge. They are payers in the sense of being delegitimized within Catholic-influenced governance venues, and excluded in that the doctrine treats their frameworks as derivative rather than as co-equal starting points for negotiation.

stakeholders.name: catholic_lay_technologists
stakeholders.situation: Catholic engineers, ethicists, and institutional actors (universities, hospital systems, NGOs) implement and translate Magisterial teaching into concrete design guidance, procurement standards, and pastoral statements. They gain professional standing and institutional backing from alignment with the doctrine, but are also bound by it — deviation risks loss of ecclesial support or institutional standing within Catholic organizations.

stakeholders.name: non_catholic_states_and_regulators
stakeholders.situation: Governments in pluralist or secular constitutional orders receive Magisterial input as one voice among many advocacy positions in AI policy consultation, without being bound to treat Catholic anthropology as authoritative. They are excluded from the doctrine's own claimed jurisdiction (it addresses consciences, not civil law directly) even though the doctrine seeks to shape their legislative outcomes indirectly through moral suasion and coalition politics.

six_questions.coordination_function: Provides a comprehensive, internally coherent normative framework — grounded in a fixed conception of the human person — that can coordinate otherwise-fragmented resistance to purely efficiency-driven or profit-driven AI deployment, giving vulnerable groups, labor advocates, and dignity-focused technologists a shared vocabulary and institutional backing they would lack individually.
six_questions.transfer_function: Moves reputational legitimacy, coalition access, and moral authority away from technocratic and transhumanist actors and toward Church-aligned institutions and their lay allies; moves attention and policy-drafting influence toward Magisterial teaching offices and away from secular ethics frameworks that decline to accept a theological starting premise.
six_questions.absent_voices: Non-Christian religious traditions with their own dignity concepts (Islamic, Buddhist, Ubuntu-derived frameworks) are largely absent from the doctrine's own textual tradition despite claiming universal applicability through natural law reasoning; AI systems' own stakeholders in non-Catholic-majority regions where the doctrine has negligible institutional reach are effectively unaddressed by its enforcement mechanisms.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: The Church's advocates would say vulnerable populations lose a powerful institutional voice against purely commercial AI deployment and labor rights framing would weaken in policy debates; secular and techno-optimist actors would say governance conversations become more procedurally neutral and less encumbered by contested theological premises, and would proceed largely as before since Magisterial teaching carries no binding civil force in most jurisdictions already.
six_questions.founding_problem: Perceived moral vacuum in AI governance debates dominated by market logic and state security interests, lacking any settled account of what a human being fundamentally is and why algorithmic treatment of persons has limits — a problem the Church frames as recurring across industrial modernity (its own genealogy running from Rerum Novarum's response to labor exploitation through to contemporary bioethics and now AI).
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: Catholic social teaching bodies and allied labor advocates attest the vacuum is real and worsening as AI deployment accelerates unchecked by any anthropological floor. Secular ethicists and pluralist scholars outside the Church attest that the vacuum is being filled by rights-based, procedural, and multi-stakeholder frameworks (UNESCO AI ethics recommendation, OECD AI principles) that do not require theological premises, and that the Magisterium's claim of unique or superior authority to fill this vacuum is itself the contested element, not the existence of a governance gap.

commentary.kernel_context: This constraint instantiates the magisterial_integralist_reading of the human_dignity_ai_governance kernel: dignity as ontological gift (imago Dei), knowable through faith and reason together, with the Magisterium claiming unique interpretive authority over what AI governance must respect. Sibling readings — secular_humanist (dignity via rational autonomy and law, no religious authority), techno_optimist (dignity enhanced through augmentation, minimal governance), and pluralist_pragmatic (dignity as contested, negotiated overlapping consensus) — are separate constraints, not alternative measurements of this one. Where this reading treats theological grounding as making dignity non-negotiable, the secular_humanist reading treats any single metaphysical foundation as itself the problem to be procedurally bracketed, and the pluralist_pragmatic reading treats this reading's universalist claim as one input among several to be negotiated down. This story's ε is authored strictly for the magisterial_integralist arrangement as it exists — Church teaching offices exercising moral suasion over AI governance discourse — not for the state of affairs the reading would bring about if fully adopted.
commentary.narrative_context: The Catholic Church, through Vatican dicasteries, papal encyclicals, and initiatives like the Rome Call for AI Ethics, asserts that AI governance must be grounded in a specific theological anthropology: the human person as an imago Dei bearer possessing infinite, inalienable dignity, correctly interpreted only through the Magisterium's teaching authority applying faith and reason together. This positions the Church as a necessary normative authority over technology development, in tension with purely secular, market-driven, or pluralist governance approaches. The doctrine offers real coordination benefits to labor advocates and vulnerable-population advocates who lack an alternative unifying framework, while imposing reputational and legitimacy costs on technocratic and transhumanist actors whose projects it explicitly names as incompatible with correct anthropology.
key_agents: the_magisterium: agenda-setting institutional authority claiming interpretive supremacy over AI-relevant dignity questions
vulnerable_populations, industrial_workers, families_and_children: named beneficiaries of the doctrine's protective anthropology
technocratic_platform_elites, transhumanist_researchers: named targets whose projects the doctrine holds as dignity-violating
secular_ai_ethicists: rival framework-holders delegitimized by the doctrine's metaphysical exclusivity claim
non_catholic_states_and_regulators: analytical observers outside the doctrine's claimed jurisdiction who receive it as one advocacy voice
commentary.logic_rationale: Extractiveness is authored as moderate (0.42) because the doctrine imposes real reputational, coalition-access, and legitimacy costs on technocratic and transhumanist actors, but enforcement is entirely non-coercive — moral suasion, institutional exclusion from Catholic-aligned venues, and appeal to conscience, with no capacity for civil sanction. Suppression is correspondingly low-moderate (0.28): alternative frameworks are not banned or criminalized, merely delegitimized within Church-influenced venues, and actors retain full exit into secular or pluralist policy spaces. Theater ratio is moderate (0.3) reflecting genuine doctrinal development (encyclicals, Vatican summits) alongside a real performative element — signatory pledges and symbolic commitments from tech firms that do not bind actual product design. Accessibility collapse is moderate (0.35): alternatives to the doctrine's framework are readily available in secular and pluralist venues, they are simply excluded from specifically Catholic-influenced spaces. Resistance is moderate-high (0.55) because the doctrine's claim to interpretive supremacy over a metaphysically contested question draws active pushback from secular ethicists and transhumanist advocates who reject its exclusive authority claim outright.
commentary.directionality_logic: Vulnerable populations, workers, and families are structural beneficiaries — the doctrine's anthropology is explicitly constructed to protect their embodied, relational personhood against algorithmic reduction — but their exit options remain trapped/constrained regardless of whether the doctrine succeeds, meaning their benefit is contingent and largely rhetorical rather than a guaranteed transfer. Technocratic elites and transhumanist researchers are named targets bearing reputational costs, but their institutional power and global mobility give them substantial exit — they can operate in jurisdictions or venues where Magisterial teaching carries no weight, which caps how extractive the constraint can actually be against them (mobile exit damps effective extraction even though the base structural relationship names them as victims).
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The founding problem — absence of a settled anthropological floor in AI governance dominated by commercial and security logics — is genuinely contested rather than obviously dead: AI deployment continues to accelerate with limited anthropological grounding in most governance frameworks, so the coordination function the doctrine claims to serve retains some live basis. What is more contested is whether the Magisterium's specific claim to *unique* authority over that gap remains warranted given the proliferation of secular and multi-stakeholder frameworks (UNESCO, OECD) addressing similar concerns without theological premises — this is not simple mandatrophy (function atrophied, mandate persists) so much as a live jurisdictional contest over who gets to fill an acknowledged gap.
commentary.perspectival_gap: From the agenda-setter seat (the Magisterium and allied lay technologists), this reads as necessary moral leadership filling a real vacuum. From the payer seats (technocratic elites, transhumanist researchers, secular ethicists), the same structure reads as an illegitimate claim to metaphysical authority that delegitimizes their work without offering them any voice in how the doctrine's content is set — they are talked about, not negotiated with, which is the structural asymmetry a tangled-rope classification should surface even though enforcement is non-coercive.

omegas.question: Is the Magisterium's claim to unique or privileged authority over AI governance's anthropological questions itself a defensible feature of a coordination mechanism, or is it the extractive core the coordination story covers for?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Track whether Magisterial input measurably shapes binding AI policy outcomes in pluralist democracies versus merely accompanying policy processes that would have reached similar substantive conclusions via secular frameworks (UNESCO, OECD) independently.
omegas.impact: If Magisterial claims to unique authority produce no differential policy outcome beyond what secular frameworks would independently generate, the authority claim functions mainly as institutional rent-seeking (legitimacy and coalition capture) rather than genuine indispensable coordination, pushing the classification toward snare; if it demonstrably produces protections absent from secular frameworks, the coordination function is more substantive.
omegas.description: Whether the exclusivity of Magisterial authority is coordination-necessary or extraction-serving.

omegas.question: Given that enforcement relies entirely on moral suasion and voluntary adoption, does this reading's demand for 'high constraint on AI design' actually translate into structural change, or does it remain primarily rhetorical/theatrical?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Longitudinal audit of Catholic-influenced AI ethics pledges (e.g. Rome Call signatories) against actual downstream changes in product architecture, data practices, or deployment decisions at signatory firms.
omegas.impact: Low observed structural change despite pledge signatures would support a higher theater_ratio and a piton-leaning trajectory (form without function); substantial observed change would support the coordination reading and validate the moderate extractiveness score.
omegas.description: Whether voluntary doctrinal adoption produces real design constraints or symbolic compliance.

omegas.question: Is the imago Dei anthropology, as the reading claims, accessible to all persons via natural reason independent of Christian revelation (making it a genuinely universal governance foundation), or is it irreducibly particular to Christian theological commitment and merely presented as universal?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Compare doctrinal claims of natural-law accessibility against actual uptake and independent derivation of equivalent dignity principles within non-Christian philosophical and religious traditions addressing AI governance.
omegas.impact: If genuinely convergent with independently-derived non-Christian frameworks, the universality claim is stronger and the doctrine's coordination function extends further; if the convergence is largely rhetorical and the substantive content remains theologically particular, the universalist framing itself becomes part of the constraint's extractive legitimation apparatus.
omegas.description: Whether the doctrine's claimed universal accessibility via reason holds up against its particular theological content.

network.dual_formulation_note: This story is one of four sibling readings decomposing the natural-language concept 'human dignity in AI governance' per the ε-invariance principle. Each reading names a structurally distinct claim about the ground of dignity and the legitimate authority to adjudicate it, with different beneficiary/victim structures and different ε: magisterial_integralist_reading (this story, moderate ε ~0.42, theological grounding, Church authority), secular_humanist_reading (rights/law grounding, democratic authority), techno_optimist_reading (augmentation grounding, minimal governance authority), pluralist_pragmatic_reading (negotiated grounding, procedural authority). All four are linked via affects_constraints because they compete for the same governance discourse space and each reading's institutional traction structurally affects the others' legitimacy and resource access — e.g., growing Magisterial influence in EU policy circles measurably reduces the pluralist_pragmatic reading's claim to be the only viable non-parochial compromise.
